title: Extra Equipamentos e Exportação Ltda. v. Case Corporation
lead: A Brazilian distributor negotiated a release with a parent-company officer acting for the subsidiary, then alleged promises made without intent to perform. The majority treated a negotiated nonreliance clause as fatal to fraud, while the dissent distinguished written commitments expressly preserved by that clause.

actors.name: Extra Equipamentos e Exportação
actors.role: Brazilian equipment distributor and fraud plaintiff

actors.name: Case Corporation and Case Brasil
actors.role: American parent defendant and Brazilian distribution subsidiary

actors.name: James Sharman
actors.role: Parent vice president signing for the subsidiary

proceedings: After a prior joinder dismissal was reversed, the district court granted Case summary judgment and costs. The Seventh Circuit affirmed both fraud dispositions, reversed the written-translation costs component, and remanded costs on September 3, 2008.
limits: The court did not determine Brazilian damages or find the alleged promises honestly made. Ordinary fraud was resolved unanimously; promissory fraud divided the panel two to one. Currency descriptions of the negotiated cap differed between the majority and dissent.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A distributorship dispute led to a negotiated release
sections.cue: Introduce the parties and what each side sought.
paragraphs: Case Brasil, a wholly owned Brazilian subsidiary of Case Corporation, hired Extra Equipamentos e Exportação as distributor in 1992. In 1999 Extra sued it in Brazil over allegedly corrupt charge-backs and opposed a merger before Brazilian authorities. Case wanted information allowing removal of corrupt subsidiary employees without employment liability.

Extra president Briante negotiated in Illinois with Case vice president James Sharman, who signed for Case Brasil despite working for the parent. No subsidiary employee attended or signed. The release ended the first Brazilian litigation, capped past-due claims, and required cooperation about corruption and withdrawal of merger objections. The majority described a $2 million cap, while Judge Ripple’s detailed account used R$2 million; those currencies were not equated.

Ripple described a full day in a Waukegan airplane hangar with Extra’s Brazilian and American commercial lawyers and financial adviser. He also identified written promises to supply standard Commercial Representative and Technical Services agreements and reverse charge-backs.

sections.title: Termination produced a second Brazilian case and American fraud claims
sections.cue: Explain the disputed promise and procedural history.
paragraphs: Extra alleged that Sharman orally promised continued distributorship in good standing with no intent to honor it. It claimed the parent used the corporate distinction to obtain information and releases while allowing the subsidiary to evade the exchange. Case Brasil later terminated the relationship, prompting another Brazilian suit. The majority reported a contract-breach determination with specific performance denied and damages still being determined. Case disputed nonperformance; Ripple stressed that the summary-judgment record had not definitively resolved repudiation and described alleged pressure to accept much greater debt and surrender the cap.

Extra sued the American parent for fraud in 2001. The district court initially dismissed for failure to join Case Brasil as indispensable, but a 2004 appeal reversed and allowed discovery. On remand, summary judgment principally relied on nonreliance, with approximately $116,000 in costs. The parties agreed Illinois substantive law governed this 2008 appeal.

sections.title: The negotiated text addressed reliance separately from integration
paragraphs: The release said the parties relied on their own judgment, knowledge, and selected lawyers rather than the other party’s or representatives’ statements, except representations and warranties expressed in the release. A separate integration clause superseded prior negotiations.

Judge Posner, joined by Judge Rovner, explained that integration and parol evidence principally protect contractual writings from contradictory negotiated terms. Acknowledging uncertainty in Illinois law, he assumed those devices alone did not bar a negotiation-fraud tort. Fraud had different pleading, proof, timing, and remedies but could also become a way to obtain omitted contract terms. Nonreliance directly addressed an element necessary to fraud: an ignored statement could not cause injury. The particular oral promise of continued distributorship emphasized by the majority was absent from the writing.

sections.title: Sophisticated negotiation made the claimed reliance unreasonable
sections.cue: Give the limits and parent-subsidiary response.
paragraphs: The majority recognized that an unrepresented lay signer might not understand technical reliance language. Without deciding whether Illinois required inquiry into circumstances, it assumed such an inquiry and found no reasonable jury could find misunderstanding. Briante ran a very large enterprise and had experienced Brazilian and New York commercial lawyers. Extra did not allege they misunderstood, failed to explain, or were misled about the clause. This was not proof of incomprehensible boilerplate or a categorical rule against every signer’s fraud suit.

Extra argued Sharman represented the parent, not the release’s named subsidiary. He expressly signed for and represented Case Brasil in procuring the agreement, and both companies could benefit. Actual or apparent authority to bind the subsidiary was inconsistent with excluding his statements merely because another company employed him. The term representative also extended beyond authority to consummate a transaction.

Even if the clause were contractually unenforceable, its language and informed negotiation made contrary oral reliance unreasonable as a tort matter. Authority to sign and reasonable reliance were separate; lack of authority would not make oral reliance reasonable.

sections.title: The majority also questioned the distinct injury theory
paragraphs: Extra did not seek rescission and disclaimed a theory undoing an induced contract. The majority saw claimed termination loss already pursued in Brazilian contract litigation without explanation of how the oral promise increased it or how Extra would have fared better without the release. It therefore found neither valid reliance nor a necessary distinct injury path. That was its characterization, disputed by Ripple, not a finding that every alleged representation was true.

sections.title: Ripple would send the written-promise scheme to a jury
sections.cue: Explain the clause’s exception and the proposed damages.
paragraphs: Ripple agreed with judgment on ordinary fraud but would reverse promissory fraud. Illinois ordinarily rejected a false future promise alone but permitted it within a fraudulent scheme, requiring knowing deception, inducement, justifiable reliance, injury, and the scheme. He found sufficient evidence for trial, noting the district court had rejected Case’s alternative arguments that scheme or causation evidence was missing.

Crucially, the clause preserved reliance on representations and warranties in the release. Distribution-related agreements, reversed charge-backs, and the cap were written commitments. Applying their express exception kept litigation anchored to negotiated text. Ripple saw allegations of a scheme to obtain irrevocable cooperation and concessions while arranging subsidiary nonperformance. Near-immediate reneging, threats to credit and spare parts, and a proposed novation from R$2 million to R$10,365,000 supported trial, not an already established fraud finding.

Rescission could not retrieve disclosed corruption information or restore abandoned merger opposition, and released Brazilian claims might be blocked by time or laches. Damages could compensate those lost opportunities. Ripple did not find those time bars actually established; he regarded them as reasons not to foreclose the damages theory.

sections.title: Costs required a narrower statutory correction
sections.cue: State the controlling merits and costs results.
paragraphs: The court rejected withholding all costs to punish Case for late presentation of its successful defense; summary cost assessment was not an inquiry into strategy. Approximately $8,700 in reporter attendance fees qualified as necessary transcript expenses.

Nearly $76,000 in translation-related charges required correction. Section 1920(6)’s interpreter compensation covered oral translation, not written exhibits. Expansive meanings of interpret did not enlarge the statutory noun or its selective list, and potentially unlimited document translation complicated administration. The conflict with a Sixth Circuit decision prompted full-court circulation; no judge requested en banc consideration, and Flaum did not participate.

The September 3, 2008 judgment affirmed both fraud rulings, with Ripple dissenting only on promissory fraud, and remanded costs after reversing the improper component. It did not cancel all costs. Rehearing and rehearing en banc were denied September 29, with Flaum’s nonparticipation recorded and no additional opinion.
